description: How the internet looks from RealUptime's check regions right now (https://realuptime.io/outages/internet-weather): for each of the ten regions (iad = US-East, sjc = US-West, fra = Europe, nrt = Asia-Pacific, ord = US-Central, yyz = Canada, lhr = UK, sin = Southeast Asia, syd = Australia, gru = South America), the latest hour's p50/p95/p99 response time across the ~195 public services in RealUptime's outage catalog, the region's 7-day baseline, and a `state` of "normal" / "slower" (only after three consecutive hours over 1.5x the baseline, clearing at 1.25x) / "no_baseline" / "no_data", plus a 24-hour sparkline and the last 30 days per day. This is a picture of a REGION's vantage point over many services, NOT any one service's latency and NOT customer monitoring traffic (which never enters this aggregate). `coverage.typical_claim_allowed` says whether the record is old enough (30 days) to call a figure "typical for the region"; until it is, say "compared with the last 7 days" instead. Takes no arguments. Readings are RealUptime's own check readings, never user reports. For a service whose status feed we can read, `vendor.feed_working` is true and `vendor` holds the vendor's own declared incident from its status page: that statement leads and gives the verdict and plate, and `checks_reading` and `vendor.regional_reading` are our check reading beside it, never a second outage. Where we cannot read a feed (`vendor.feed_working` false), the answer is our checks alone. "blocked" means our check was refused, which is NOT a failed check of the service. A no-data answer is never a passing check. Our check readings are our own reading from outside, not the service's official status. `check_evidence`, when it is not null, says what a pass of this service's check shows and does not show: repeat it with any claim that the service works. Cite the returned source.url when repeating any of this.
name: internet_weather
